[h1]+Pros+[/h1]
+Good Mod Support
+Realism
+Great representation of modern warfare
+Great information and details about unit formation, weaponry, vehicles, etc.
+Great representation of multiple biomes and cycles of the day
+Sounds and looks amazing -- even if outdated 


[h1]-Cons-[/h1]
-Bugs
-Horrible loading times
-Performance issues
-AI is problematic


[h1]The Narrative[/h1]
There isn’t a story per se, but multiple operations that take place in Chernarus and Takistan. You’ll be in charge of a squadron of men or an elite unit during night operations. You’ll also be leading the cavalry across the deserts and the helicopters in the skies. Each operation is well detailed on what needs to be done. They’ll explain who the enemy is, where the enemy may potentially be placed at, what you’ll be doing, and what needs to be done in order to achieve victory. 

There will also be dialogues between soldiers, HQ/FoB and all other parties involved throughout each operation – making the missions feel life-like and making you feel as if you were a lieutenant in charge of his squad. The additional dialogue about enemy movements, soldiers being injured, and giving orders to your fellow soldiers only adds to the narrative.


[h1]The Gameplay[/h1]
The tutorial well help understand the fundamental aspects, such as movement controls, giving orders to units, how to fire weapons, and a multitude of other options that most first-person shooters can only dream of. You’ll understand the concepts of stealth, urban warfare, and traditional warfare in open fields with an array of armaments. The weather and day/night cycles can either hinder or give the advantage during combat. The gameplay is complex and challenging onto itself because there is so much to learn. This isn’t a game that you can learn everything within one day; it'll take some time to understand the basics.

You can choose to be in first-person or in third-person view – depending on the scenario. Some missions prevent you from going into third-person in order to experience the game in an immersive environment. The problem with third-person view is you can see someone around the wall or hiding behind the corner even though you should not be able to see them (I can understand why certain missions disabled this feature).

You'll have to look at the map and find opportunities to attacks, flanking maneuvers, ambushes; commanding fellow soldiers to attack at specific times in order to engage the enemy with minimal loses, and even go door-to-door breaches where killing a civilian can end the mission. 

The gameplay also requires patience and a desire to learn the abundance of menus that this game offers. Personally, I still don’t have a clue what half of them do, but those who have mastered the game are a force to be reckoned with. You will also require some perseverance as this game is unrewarding to those who charge into battle headstrong. 


[h1]The Content[/h1]
You’ll have an arsenal of weapons and vehicles at your disposal – or what is allowed during said scenarios. The guns are based off those of multiple companies throughout the world; guns that are used by the U.S. Military and fellow NATO alliance members. These also include vehicles used by the U.S. Military – either mentioned by aviation, cavalry, and maritime means. You’ll also witness multiple arsenal variants from the Eastern European nations.

You’ll have an array of equipment to help you along your operations. These will include maps, ammo, med-kits; a large array of explosive weaponry (e.g. standard grenades, rocket launchers, javelins, etc.), and other forms of equipment (e.g. flash/smoke grenades, binoculars, body armor, etc.). You’ll experience a lot of the arsenal while manning your guns on the ground, flying in the air, or driving multiple vehicles on your operations. 

You’ll see fictional lands that resemble areas like Eastern Europe or the deserts of the Middle East. You’ll engage in moments when the day gradually shifts into night and it happens right in front of your eyes or when the weather kicks in to lessen your visibility. There will also be devices such as thermal, infrared, and night vision. This game has a lot to offer in terms of military content, their specifications, factions, detailed mission logs, and anything else to add to make the game as real as possible. 

The purpose of this content is to make you feel like you’re actually in combat, without actually leaving the comfort of your chair. Is it perfect? No, but there is no reload in real life either. I know a few veterans who have played this game (one being my father) and they say the game covers a lot of the realism, but it will never compete with actual realistic warfare. If you want true realism, then join the armed forces. For those of you that have served, I thank you for your service.  


[h1]The Auditory[/h1]
Having fired off handguns in the past, the sounds of the weapons and the vehicles shooting at their targets are amazing for being dated at 2010. Honestly, that isn't a bad aspect since a lot of modern shooters sound like paintball guns. The sounds are crisp, delightful, and impactful. You hear that whistling sound? Hide because that’s a mortar. 

Even the voice actors put some military spirit when acting out their roles. You can hear the stern voice of a commander to an inexperienced private saying, “Yes, Sir!” It helps portray that realism in the game to show that everyone is different and some may even be nervous or stern as an ox without a care that a bullet almost hit them. 


[h1]The Visual Design[/h1]
The graphics are outdated and didn’t really age well with time. The main purpose of the game is to be realistic and not be in the spotlight for having some of the best visual designs on the planet. Some may criticize the game for its lack of visual appeal, such as lighting effects, shadows, and even the assets used to formulate a rendered object. Yet, the game still offers a charming appearance: 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2446042104

At times the graphics will look rather dry – such as a helicopter blowing up and then immediately being burnt to a crisp. Again, this game is about simulation, not benchmark graphic design. I rather enjoyed the graphics despite being slightly outdated, and enjoyed the visual design regardless.


[h1]The Performance and Functionality[/h1]
When controlling your soldiers (platoon/cavalry) sometimes their AI acts incredibly stupid. You’ll have to repeat the commands several times in order for them to behave the way you want and act accordingly to your strategic maneuvers. The pathfinding can also become a problematic element as your unit members will get stuck in buildings, behind rocks and trees (mainly vehicles), or try to go uphill knowing logically they cannot. Even if you set up the waypoints for them to walk/drive in that particular order, they still find a way to become a headache.

The game also displays some severe performance issues. Such issues pertain to loss of frame rates, long loading times, and graphical glitches that the AI can perform (e.g. walking though walls). On average I would get around 57 FPS. There are also bugs throughout some of the missions that will make you reload your last checkpoint or have you redo the entire mission again. My issue pertains to the game somehow corrupting itself and deleting my saved files.


[h1]The Technical Specifications[/h1]
OS: Windows 7
CPU: i7-4790k
GPU: GeForce GTX 1080
Ram: 16GB


[h1]The Verdict[/h1]
Between the realism and immersion that I felt while playing this game, I enjoyed it for the most part. The complex controls were off-putting till I got used to them, and then I understood how to proceed better with the missions later on. Yes, there are bugs and they can be frustrating – especially if you have to restart a mission, but for the most part, I had an overall enjoyable experience with the game.

[b]ARMA II: Operation Arrowhead[/b] is best known for the popular zombie mod DayZ, which is a unique apocalyptic open-world experience.

But what many of the players who bought the game only to try DayZ miss out on, is the vanilla game itself and the original experience when you join an organized clan or server to teamwork with other players during tactical missions. All servers use unique player-created missions.

The missions are normally PvE, but PvP also exist to a lesser extent. Missions can range from being in an escort of military vehicles, rescue hostages, or attack/defend outposts. The game has a built-in mission editor that is easy to manage. ARMA II have plenty of realistic weapons, vehicles and characters. There are also hundreds of mods that increase the amount of everything.

The game suits people who like sandbox, simulations and action games. However, it's not a very fast-paced game like the CoD or BF-series. In the ARMA-series, you might die unless the wound is treated. You have no visible healthbar and you require a map and GPS to know where you are.

This is probably my favorite game of all time. I never played a game more than this one and I will say why in this review.

Back in 2011 or 2012 I remember being bored and looking for new games to play since I was new to PC gaming and always played on Consoles before this. I remember coming across a YouTube video about Arma 2 realism shooting. I thought it was interesting since I grew up playing Halo and COD when I was a kid. I seen this was something new so I thought to give it a go. I came for the realism but stayed when I noticed a server called "Cherno life". I had no idea what it was but it sounded interesting. 

--- My RP Experience ---

I load into the server and I see there are Cops and Civilians. I learned that day what a online RP game was like back then. It was the funniest thing I have ever seen. People playing as Cops and chasing people who would rob a bank or gas station or commit murder. Even things like speeding got you pulled over. I never seen anything like it and I just loved it. I remember one day I got tired of some people playing as Cops just doing stupid things like killing civs for no reason and it annoyed me but I was in luck. I came across a video that had "City Life RPG" as the title. It was a mod and the very first I went and downloaded. It had things like sports cars and even shitty 1979 Honda Civics in the game and if you couldn't afford that than I guess you could test your luck on stealing a car but the cops could find out and you could be put in jail and that isn't fun.

There was just so much to do in that mod, you could grow drugs and run a business doing it. You could do the boring legal route to and sell olives which hardly made money but it wasn't illegal. Fishing and illegal fishing (shark hunting) was a thing and if you wanted to just be clean you could even become a cop which was hard as hell to do in this server. Robbing banks was even a choice but usually a stupid one unless you had snipers or were good at tricking the cops otherwise it wasn't worth it. It was pretty much GTA but with real people instead of A.I

I put at least 1000+ hours into that mod because it was so different and niche that it just appealed to me. I even met people on there who I still talk to today 5 years later. The mod just had one of the best communites ever and nothing comes close to it for me. Like I said in the beginning, I came for the realism side of the game but the RP side I accidently came across kept me playing it for a very long time.


--- DayZ Mod ---
When I started playing Arma 2, I remember there being 4 DayZ servers. They weren't that popular either but I tried it one day and I loved the idea and the game itself. It was something that has never been done back then. I remember this mod just blowing up and 4 servers became a 1000 in 2 months. Arma 2 went from a niche game with 4,000 people playing at most to one of the top PC games out there all thanks to this mod. Survival games have been changed forever because of the success of this mod that was made into a full standalone years later and is still one of the biggest Early Access titles in history. DayZ was fun with friends but after a few months of playing it and things like Overpoch, EPoch started coming out and all the hackers started joining it kind of going annoying. Combat logging was huge back then to which ruined the mod for me but in the beginning I think it was one of the best mods ever to release.

--- Realism Mods ---
Played some realism mods for a bit because that is what I was looking for in Arma 2 in the first place. Mods made it so fun to play and for awhile I enjoyed it. I did this for around 3 months and just got tired of the ego some people had. The community kind of ruined it for me but overall I still enjoyed it. Some of the best mods I have ever seen in a game like DayZ so this was nothing short of incredible.

I said this before and I will say it again. My favorite game of all time. One of the best communites (in some mods, DayZ was pretty bad after awhile.) and the best mods I have ever seen created in any game.

A Game that holds much history not only to me but to the gaming community as a whole.

ArmA is or rather was a popular game between 2012 to 2016 due to it's spike in popularity on YouTube that raised widespread attention to an untouched market of an enhanced military combat simulator featuring it's enormous map size that could be traversed in real-time by land, sea or air through methods of transportation such as military and civilian vehicles, helicopters, planes, buses, drones, jets and others. This was not a common concept at the time as games were still quite linear and didn't provide such diversity that allowed up to 100 other people to be on the same map and interact with each other.

The above is what set the baseline for the game and it gathered a small following, the biggest change was the Mod scene that was introduced which allowed people to create diverse campaign modes, custom maps, custom vehicles, custom weapons, custom accessories, custom communication and diverse movement and so forth...

This modding scene is what escalated the game to a further level and made it truly a one of a kind experience as everybody had a chance to show off and experiment with custom features that can be shared to others and create something by the name of Mod Packs.

One of these Mod Packs was called Exile. This mod added zombies, base-building, custom missions, currency, raiding, parachuting, safe-zones, trading and others. This is where the game was truly at it's peak and what it's synonymous for hence why there is still a small dedicated player base.

The game at it's current state is mostly forgotten about, everybody has moved onto it's sequel ArmA 3 which enhances every aspect of the game and modding scene and makes the game run much smoother on an updated engine and provides more Quality of Life improvements.

Definitely a game that had a good run and brought about many memories for many people and the interactions and action that came out from the times spent playing with friends is something that is memorable.

Arma 2: Operation Arrowhead feels genuinely unique compared to Arma 3. I have a lot of respect for Arma 3, but I never really connected with its vanilla futuristic setting. OA's more grounded modern-military atmosphere has a character of its own, and after spending time with both games, I still find myself coming back to Operation Arrowhead.
One of the biggest reasons is the modding scene. Arma 2 had a tremendous amount of mods available through Armaholic. It's honestly a shame that Armaholic was taken down, because it was such an important part of the Arma community and made discovering all those mods incredibly easy. These days, you can still find a lot of content on Mod DB and ArmedAssault.info, at least as far as I remember, but it isn't quite the same experience but the mission editor and SQF scripting are the real reason I have spent so many hours in this game.

The editor gives you an almost ridiculous amount of freedom. You can create practically any scenario you can imagine: custom missions, dynamic battles, experiments, scripted events, AI encounters, campaigns, and whatever else you can come up with. And the more you learn SQF, the more you realize that the limits aren't really the editor itsef ,they're mostly your own knowledge and creativity. that's what makes OA special to me. It's not just a military sandbox; it's a game where you can spend hundred of hours building your own game inside the game.

the engine has its problems. Arma 2 is notorious for not making particularly good use of modern multi-core CPUs, and performance can suffer badly in certain situations. Arma 3 improved things somewhat in this regard, although performance has never exactly been the series' strongest point. still, despite its age and technical shortcomings, Arma 2: Operation Arrowhead has an atmosphere and flexibility that I don't think Arma 3 completely replaced.

If you're interested in military sandboxes, mission making, scripting, or just messing around with an incredibly flexible game engine, OA is still worth experiencing.

Introduction:

ArmA 2: Operation Arrowhead is the standalone DLC (Downloadable Content) Pack for ArmA 2, A Military Simulator by Czech developer Bohemia Interactive. ArmA 2: OA is the only standalone DLC pack for ArmA 2. Multiple other DLC packs play part in Takistan, Including the BAF (British Armed Forces) DLC and PMC (Private Military Contractors) DLC.

The Map(s):

ArmA 2: OA is set in the fictional Middle-Eastern country of Takistan. Takistan has many towns, villages and cities to explore, with two airfields on either end of the map. The map of Zargabad, A Small desert city in the middle of nowhere, quite small compared to Chernarus or Takistan, but the city is hugh compared to Takistan's largest, Rasman. Zargabad also comes with an airfield and a few buildings here and there. the PMC and BAF DLCs use this map as well.

The Gameplay:

ArmA 2, as a military simulator has many aspects involved in succeeding. To me, and many others, the most important is Teamwork. You have to work as a team to get things done in this game, and I love that consept. It is very slow paced, very tactical, and aimed at people that don't like to get things done rambo-style. Movement is extremely fiddly with the inability to walk through clearly enterable spaces and breaking your legs on the oddest of places. The game is fairly old, however, coming in at a 2010 release, a year after the original ArmA 2.

Graphics/Voice Acting:

Graphics and Voice Acting are quite shameful, but the game is old and developed by a Czech developer making an english game, and the quality is tolerable.

The Multiplayer:

The ArmA Multiplayer is quite easily where the most fun is to be had. With excessive mods and gamemodes developed plus the original gamemodes implemented to play with your friends, i've spent 99% of my OA Experience on the Multiplayer. My most enjoyable moments on the multiplayer moments were on Takistan Life: Revolution servers. TLR, as it is abbreviated to, is a Roleplay Mission File for OA.

My Issue(s):

My only Issue with OA is the fact that when update 1.63 was released, it wiped out an extremely large fraction of all multiplayer servers. I took this as a sign of BI telling us to go to ArmA 3, which is quite rude. Luckily, servers are popping back up here and there, which is a very good sign.

Summary:

Overall, All ArmA games are amazing in my opinion, but ArmA 2: OA gets the cake. Congratulations to Bohemia Interactive for making such an enjoyable, but serious game and I hope this review was found helpful.

'Do you recommend this game,' Steam asks me. I do, emphatically. I hope this anecdote from an in-game multiplayer experience I had will explain why. Prepare yourself for [u]ARMA2: The Review: The Movie.[/u]

Spring, 2011; early in my ARMA career, first tour of duty after a Steam Sale. I'm a fairly fresh recruit, seasoned with a couple dozen game-hours spent trudging through an expansive and swampy learning curve. Spent today at work, drove home, made dinner, cleaned up; it's Game-O'clock. Steam. ARMA2. Launch. Menu surfing, looking for multiplayer. Server browser hits my face with lists of information. -AWP-Warfare [i]Capture the Island[/i] mode looks appealing tonight. Played it a couple times before, and I feel comfortable with the basics by now. Server connection established.

Click! I'm in, filling the boots of a digital NATO badass. Apparently, international treaty organisations occasionally require the service of men with guns. Disturbing thought, but I'm no politician. I'm just a nobody with a rifle, taking orders that filter down the food chain. Those orders fill my mind now. Objective: town. Location: nearby...as the crow flies. Heh, the team's commander [i]does[/i] have airborne technology unlocked, I just don't have the cash to buy a lift yet. Looks like I'm taking the scenic route. A quick check of my map tells me I'm at one of our hidden frontier bases and that there's two whole mountains between me and the nearby town. Great... I'll be taking the scenic route to the scenic route. The map tells me more: several of my team members and their A.I. controlled task forces are currently approaching the town. I'm already late for the party :(

Might as well bring the fireworks.

The base I'm at has only an armour factory and infantry barracks, but both will well suit my rapidly forming battle plan. I'm thinking heavy calibre fire support from high ground, overlooking the town. The topographic information in the map shows that the road I'll be taking is nestled around a minor hill as it approaches the town. Perfect. I'll park two BMPs there and they'll provide overwatch of the whole area while my comrades finish their capture of the town. An LAV will ferry me and one squad of A.I. infantry to the combat zone. I spend the required funds and set the plan in action.

Wait a tick, BeatYourHeadIn, are you telling me you actually have to plan how you’re going to get your troops and equipment from point A to point B in ARMA2? Logistics in a game!? Yes, actual logistics...in a game with a map so FRIGGIN’ big you need to employ logistical planning skills to see any sort of success. And it's not boring!

Back to the story. Formation of a military convoy. A few orders issued to my A.I. controlled task force later and the BMPs are on point while I lounge in the command chair of the LAV at the rear of the column. I man the turret-mounted automatic grenade launcher, a devastating weapon. Its barrel is ominously pointed at and tracking a lollygagging friendly player as my convoy departs base. [i]Yeah, that's right chump, make one wrong move and I'll end you![/i] Though itching to test the power of my new toy, I decide it's not worth getting banned over.  I let my teammate live, for now.

The A.I. drivers of my convoy are as dim as a new moon, but I can fine tune my plans and keep up with current events while they drive. It's an 10 to 15 minute (realtime) drive that negotiates a winding mountain pass through an elegant evergreen forest. These are backroads, unpaved; enemy forces unlikely to be using this route. I feel secure enough that I spend most of the trip looking at the map, reading topography, lanes of fire, positions of friendlies. I smile when I realize I could probably minimize ARMA2 and play a few rounds of Counterstrike while my convoy travels.

Dying immediately is certainly the last thing I'm worried about as I crest the peak of the second mountain.

Suddenly: EXPLOSION..DEAFENING SOUND..FROM BEHIND..MASSIVE DETONATION..JESUS H. CHRIST WHERE IS THAT VOLUME KNOB! What is going on here!?

My turret pans to the rear of the LAV. The sight, what a sight...I'll never forget. Fire. Wall. 60? 70 feet tall? A wall. Of fire. Taller than the trees in the forest, literally FILLS my view from left to right. There is nothing in view except the fire. I'm in awe. Confused. Shaken. I've seen 'splosions in this game before, BUT NEVER LIKE THAT! Did somebody tried to nuke me FFS!? I know there's no nukes in this game mode, so...

Over the cacophany of destruction: the scream of jet engines. Very close. As the flames die down, a large shape traverses the air over the crest of the crag. Airframe, Sukhoi configuration. Enemy. Wing tilted down slightly; canopy visible. I know he's surveying the carnage below him. Hunting me. Cursing his aim when he sees the LAV still intact. I feel small, molecule small; what I just witnessed was caused by his war machine. Napalm bombs. Heavy ordinance. Whatever it was, it dealt complete destruction to that forest.

Understand this, readers: in this game, air superiority is a literal phrase. Air is SUPERIOR in this game. This isn't your Battlefield "oh look I can shoot a few rockets from my jet fighter and maybe kill one or two goofs on the ground and then reload (because reloading rockets on a flying jet makes a lot of sense) and kill a couple more goofs" experience. No! In ARMA your aircraft can have a payload of more than a hundred devastating rockets and you can fire 'em full auto like a machine gun and destroy an entire town worth of goofs on the ground if you wanted to. Ha! Forget about balance! This is the real life Shiznit. Modern air forces don't invest heavily in war planes because they're "balanced". They invest in them because they can kill a hell of a lot of people quickly! ARMA2 knows this. Simply put, the developers have a big Bohemian boner for air power.

But BeatYourHeadIn, what happened next? Tell us! Okay, I'll tell you. A miracle happened. My convoy survives the 'splosion to end all 'splosions. My battle plans go up in smoke like the forest around me. My current objective is to live through the next 30 seconds. The LAV is the only reason I'm still alive. It is damaged, but drivable. I order my drivers to haul ass in a forwardly direction. I track the Sukhoi as the convoy labours onward. The receding bogey performs a wide highspeed U-turn. He's heading straight for me again. Relentless much? He's the UPS guy we all wished was real: the one who comes back after he missed you the first time, instead of leaving a note telling you to pick up your package at the office near the airport!

Then, from beyond the first mountain I had passed: a smoke trail racing skywards. Anti-aircraft missile! Ha! RETURN TO SENDER, A-HOLE! Two vectors intersect in a puff of smoke and light. Direct hit! Booyah! Wait, uh... he's still flying at me. HEY! HE'S STILL FLYING AT ME!

With black smoke billowing out of his engines, this topgun is still determined to deliver my severance package. Frantically, I order the BMPs to target the limping jet. Cannon rounds arc through the sky in attempt to smite the airborne menace. Sukhoi Dude is getting closer, but he's losing altitude. Fast. He's now descending below my level on the mountain, looking up at me through the trees as he approaches. None of the BMP fire connects, but it doesn't matter. THIS GOOSE IS COOKED BOYS! Relief. Now, his desperation salvo of rocket fire is way off-target; falls harmlessly some distance away. I watch him frantically yaw right and nose up as his fighter loses the last of its life-sustaining lift and plummets in a sideways cartwheel into the trees. The inferno he leaves behind is a feast for the eyes. There was nothing left but a dark crater.
Now, I can start thinking about that town again...

What, are you apes gonna dig him a grave!? We got our own mission to die for! Forward march!

All that's left to say is: play this game!

What can I say? It's the one and the only ArmA II: Operation Arrowhead, probably one of the most well known games amongst the PC gaming community. This game has everything for everyone. You want to stroll around in a zombie infested wasteland full of players trying to kill you instead of zombies? It's got that! You want to fly in a special ops raid on an insurgent filled town at night with the glow of green illuminating your room while tracers fly on the screen? It's got that! You want to play as an abusive cop and beat down the local civilian population for driving in the middle of the road? It has that too. Yes ArmA II:Operation Arrowhead has just about everything you could ask for, but it does have stuff you didn't ask for. Like AI's that are either blind of Vasili Zaitsev, Zombies that come through walls to get you, and other weird glitches that although are not game breaking, are annoying at the best of times. 

Whatever your fortay me be in video games, I am sure that Operation Arrowhead can fullfil many of your hopes and expectations from a now old, military simulator that is at the top of its respected genre of games. Whether you want to be a pilot, infantry soldier, tank operator, marksmen, civilian, rebel, or police officer this game can give you what you want. It is for these reasons and more that you will discover, that I recommend this game even so long after its initial release.
